tier_reason: Public benchmark code against the named C++ baseline (bench_cpp/benches/compare.rs, Criterion, seeded inputs; C++ compiled by bench_cpp/build.rs with cc opt_level(3), -DNDEBUG, -std=c++11; Rust bench profile inherits bench_cpp/Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true, codegen-units = 1), compilers named (rustc 1.99.0, Apple clang 17.0.0) and CPU named (Apple M2 Pro), so it meets A. First-party run, which the A rubric allows.

corrections.claimed_speedup: bench_cpp/README.md (Criterion point estimates, ms, one run of the full suite, Apple M2 Pro): Uniform(1,3) n=110,000 k=5 rust_indices 13.2 / rust_optimal 14.5 vs cpp_linear 26.0 / cpp_loglinear 25.3; k=20 49.7 / 52.7 vs 105.3 / 90.7; n=1,000,000 k=5 126.7 / 142.9 vs 254.9 / 249.8; k=20 513.5 / 556.1 vs 995.4 / 940.5; Uniform(0,1000) n=110,000 k=3 7.6 / 9.1 vs 16.5 / 16.1, k=50 114.4 / 120.0 vs 256.0 / 193.0; bimodal k=7 16.0 / 17.6 vs 31.3 / 28.7; BIC selection of k in 1..9 rust_optimal 26.7 vs 54.5 / 50.9 (n=110,000) and 263.1 vs 510.2 / 515.9 (n=1,000,000). The slowest Rust call (rust_optimal, which does the BIC step) against the faster C++ method is 1.6x to 1.9x faster in every row; rust_indices against the faster C++ method is 1.7x to 2.1x; the widest gap, fastest Rust against slowest C++, is 2.3x (Uniform(0,1000) k=30 and k=50) (all derived from page data). PR #41 (merged 2026-10-01) said 'Rust is 23 to 48 % faster than the C++ code in all cases'; that statement predates the 2026-10-02 commits that vectorised the split-point search, sped up the BIC step and replaced the table (a37c045).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust: rustc 1.99.0, cargo bench with the bench profile inheriting bench_cpp/Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (opt-level 3), no -C target-cpu; split-point search dispatched at run time through fearless_simd (NEON on aarch64). C++: Apple clang 17.0.0 via the cc crate in bench_cpp/build.rs with opt_level(3) (-O3), -DNDEBUG, -std=c++11, warnings off, no LTO, no -march; the 11 Ckmeans.1d.dp sources that the ckmeans-1d-dp Python package compiles plus a C shim (cpp/shim.cpp).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 12 stars, 1 fork; crates.io 'ckmeans' 23,737 downloads (1,409 recent), version 2.2.0; also published to npm as @urschrei/ckmeans (WASM)
corrections.caveats: Library win, not a language-level claim: the Rust crate and the C++ code solve the same objective and the agreement tests check identical clusters, but the implementations differ (Rust: flat matrix, stack-based divide-and-conquer column fill computing SSQ once per candidate, split-point search with four independent minima vectorised through fearless_simd; C++: SMAWK for 'linear' and scalar divide-and-conquer for 'loglinear'), so the speedup mixes algorithm constant factors, accumulator structure and explicit SIMD. The C++ call does a BIC step with Kmin = Kmax = k (6 to 10 percent of its time) that rust_indices and rust_clusters skip, writes a per-value label array in input order, and is wrapped in a Rust mutex plus an O(n) finiteness check; rust_optimal does the same BIC step and is still 1.6x to 1.9x faster. LTO and codegen-units = 1 apply to the Rust side only (C++ built as a static library without LTO); neither side sets a target CPU. Single run of the suite on one Apple M2 Pro, benchmark written by the crate author; the bench_cpp crate (2026-10-01, 5456a98) and its results were added in October 2026 commits, and PR #41 links a claude.ai/code session. The vendored C++ in bench_cpp/vendor is LGPL-3.0-or-later (benchmark only); the crate itself is BlueOak-1.0.0, which is OSI-approved per the SPDX license list 3.29.0 and includes a patent licence. The repository's Cargo badge says 'passively-maintained'.
corrections.why_faster: From the README 'Implementation' table and bench_cpp/README.md: flat contiguous DP matrix, stack-based divide-and-conquer column fill whose single-pass inner loop computes SSQ once per candidate, a pre-allocated stack reused across columns, and a split-point search that keeps four independent minima so it vectorises (fearless_simd run-time dispatch; NEON on the M2 Pro), against the scalar SMAWK and divide-and-conquer fills of Ckmeans.1d.dp. The C++ default call also spends 6 to 10 percent on a BIC step that rust_indices skips. Library engineering and SIMD, not Rust codegen.

notes: All table numbers match bench_cpp/README.md exactly; the record's derived range was wrong at the top (slowest Rust against the faster C++ method is 1.6x to 1.9x, not up to 2.3x) and the PR #41 '23 to 48 %' quote is stale, both corrected. BlueOak-1.0.0 is OSI-approved (SPDX license-list-data 3.29.0, isOsiApproved true), so usability moves from reference to copyable. Shortcomings to record: library-vs-library win with different accumulator structure and explicit SIMD (same_algorithm false), first-party single run on one laptop, LTO on the Rust side only, benchmark added in October 2026.

tier_reason: Public harness (cbench in nordlow/compiler-benchmark, MIT) with every compiler command line in code (gcc/g++/clang/clang++ at default -O0 with warning flags; c3c compile -q -O0), compiler versions in the README table (c3c 0.8.5, gcc/g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang 23.1.1) and the CPU named (AMD Ryzen AI 7 350, Arch Linux), so it meets A; upgraded from B because the flags the record could not find are in the public script, consistent with the dmd row (batch-66) and the tinycc retier on the same suite.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table (Ryzen AI 7 350), us per generated function. Total=Build+Run untemplated: C3 (c3c 0.8.5) 153 vs C gcc-15 392 (2.6x), C gcc 16.2.1 454 (3.0x), C++ g++-15 303 (2.0x), C++ g++ 16.2.1 486 (3.2x), C++ clang++ 23.1.1 236 (1.5x); C3 is 1.3x slower than C clang 23.1.1 (118). Templated: C3 255 vs g++-15 600 (2.4x) and g++ 16.2.1 566 (2.2x); 2.4x slower than clang++ templated (107). Link-free Compile column: C3 109.3 (256.6 templated) vs gcc-15 193.8 (1.8x), gcc 16.2.1 400.1 (3.7x), g++-15 269.6 / 665.0 (2.5x / 2.6x), g++ 16.2.1 372.3 / 524.8 (3.4x / 2.0x); clang 77.9 and clang++ 82.4 / 128.7 compile faster than c3c. Check column: C3 15.0 is slower than gcc -fsyntax-only (11.9 and 11.8) and clang (13.5). All ratios derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: From the public harness script cbench (./benchmark is a symlink to it; the C/C++, C3 and Odin blocks are identical in the 'benchmark' script at the table commit d16d0a5, 2026-10-09): gcc, g++, clang and clang++ get -Wall -Wextra (C) or -Wno-c++11-extensions (C++) and no -O flag, so default -O0; check uses -fsyntax-only, compile uses -c, build links through the driver's default system linker. c3c: check 'compile-only -q -O0 -C', compile 'compile-only -q -O0', build 'compile -q -O0 -o main' (c3c links with its default linker, 'cc' per its help text; the standard library is included by default). Versions: c3c 0.8.5, gcc/g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1, clang/clang++ 23.1.1. Each cell is the minimum of --run-count=10 repetitions (capped at 3 or 2 for steps over 1 s or 3 s) divided by 40,000 generated functions (200 x 200), with tasks run concurrently in a multiprocessing pool and each worker pinned to one core via os.sched_setaffinity.
corrections.hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux; README says 'as of 2026-09', tables last updated in commit d16d0a5 on 2026-10-09
corrections.stars_or_usage: 5.9k stars, 408 forks (c3lang/c3c); benchmark repo nordlow/compiler-benchmark 167 stars, 17 forks, MIT
corrections.caveats: Compile-time claim, not run-time: both sides build unoptimised code (gcc/g++/clang default -O0, c3c -O0), so the -O3 rule for run-time baselines and the crippled-baseline precedent do not apply; the win is the wave's off-baseline case and is recorded as a toolchain compile-speed entry. Not a language-level win: clang compiles the C version faster than c3c compiles the C3 version (Total 118 vs 153, Compile 77.9 vs 109.3) and clang++ templated beats C3 templated (107 vs 255), and C3's semantic check (15.0 us/f) is slower than gcc's -fsyntax-only (11.9), so the gap is GCC's -O0 code generation against c3c's LLVM -O0 path. C and C++ get -Wall -Wextra or -Wno-c++11-extensions; tcc (4), cuik (76) and cproc (86) compile C faster still. Synthetic arithmetic call chains in one translation unit with no headers, standard library or modules; the README says real builds are dominated by headers, module resolution and parallelism. Noisy cells: gcc-15 Total 392 is double its Compile 193.8, clang++ untemplated Total 236 is nearly 3x its Compile 82.4, clang++ templated Total 107 is below its Compile 128.7, and the README prose (clang 87, GCC ~418-455, c3c +77% templated) comes from a different run than the tables. The built binaries' results are never checked. Single machine, single sample run by an independent D-community developer.
corrections.why_faster: From the table: C3's front-end check is slower than gcc's (15.0 vs 11.9 us/f), and the gap opens in code generation (Compile 109.3 vs 193.8 and 400.1 us/f), i.e. c3c's LLVM -O0 backend against GCC's -O0 backend; LLVM via clang is faster still (77.9), so the speed belongs to the toolchain, not the C3 language. The README attributes the spread among compilers to backend cost (dmd vs ldmd2 vs gdc).

notes: Numbers match the README table exactly; flags read from cbench (the 'benchmark' file is a 6-byte symlink to cbench) and checked unchanged at the table commit d16d0a5. c3c MIT plus LGPL-3.0 compiler source, 5.9k stars, last commit 2026-10-10 confirmed. Record as a toolchain compile-speed entry beating GCC only (clang and tcc are faster); consider a compile-time or toolchain category rather than systems-and-safety, as for the dmd row.

corrections.caveats: Compile-time claim, not run-time: both sides build unoptimised or minimally optimised code (gcc/g++/clang default -O0, Odin default -o:minimal), so the -O3 rule for run-time baselines and the crippled-baseline precedent do not apply; recorded as a toolchain compile-speed entry. Harness asymmetry: Odin builds link with lld (-linker:lld) while gcc and g++ use the default system linker, and Odin has no link-free Compile cell, so the linker share of the gap cannot be separated; C adds -Wall -Wextra. corrections.why_faster: From the table and cbench: Odin's front-end check is slower than gcc's (19.1 vs 11.9 us/f), so the gap is in code generation and linking: Odin's LLVM backend at -o:minimal with separate build units plus lld, against GCC's -O0 backend and the default system linker. clang (LLVM, default linker) is faster than Odin, so the speed belongs to the toolchain and linker choice, not the Odin language.
